chapter: Boston roadhouses and the Army band
title: Joining the Lynnfield roadhouse band and the 'Dixie' request
summary: Leroy Johnson recommends him for a Lynnfield roadhouse; he auditions, earns good money and room and board, and a man pays $10 to hear only 'Dixie'.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: outside of Danvers and he called me up and said, 'hey, you want to come up here and play?' I said 'what?'
Danvers was up outside of Wakefield.

In Massachusetts. It was noted for an insane asylum in Danvers and this guy called me up and said 'you want to come up here and play.' That was in Lynnfield, Massachusetts. I said 'why, certainly' and he said all right, so that was a place where everybody wanted to go because that's where everybody, you know, all the big people used to come up there.

This was around 1914 and I went up there and I made an audition and I know I made a whole lot of mistakes but the man said you want the job. I said why certainly so then we had a violin player and guitar player and a drummer.
And we used to entertain and if we didn't make 10, 20 dollars a night, we weren't doing anything. Sometimes we would make around $30 a night.
In them days, the average working person was making about that much a week.

Oh, yeah, we were getting $15 a week room and board, see, they roomed us out there. They had a nice bungalow for all the musicians but when we'd get in there, we'd get on the floor at 7 o'clock, start working and we worked till 12 and if people didn't give us any money, we'd go out to the bar and hang out at the bar and I remember Mrs. Eggleston she was the boss, she used to come out to the bar and say, Mr. Whaley, would you come and give us some music.

I said, them people don't want our music. They ain't interested in music. So after awhile I'd go back out and we'd get together and then you'd hear, people would come up or send the waiter up, here's a $5 bill, here's -- play so and so.

I remember one day a little short fellow, he was in all beard and he had a Prince Albert suit coat on and he came up and says, hey I want you to play 'Dixie'. I said okay and he went in his pocket and pulled out his wallet and give me a $10 bill. He said, 'play nothing but 'Dixie.' I said okay. So we kept on playing 'Dixie' and people hey don't you know anything else. This man is paying me $10 to play that, so then they started giving me money.
We used to make a whole lot of money.
Do you remember any of the songs other than Dixie was popular during that time?
Row, Row, Row, 'Oh, You Beautiful Doll.'
